mainTopic: Why חזקה takes three years, whether the years must be consecutive, and how to prove day-and-night use of a house.
overview: The גמרא first rejects an attempt to learn the three-year rule of חזקה from a פסוק in ירמיה, because the prophet was only giving good advice. רבא then tries several logical reasons. First he says an owner forgives two years but not three, then that he doesn't bother protesting until the third year. אביי knocks down each of these. רבא's final reason is that people keep their deeds safe for about three years, so after that, use of the land takes the deed's place. A protest made when the holder isn't there still counts, because word spreads from friend to friend. רב הונא rules that the three years must be back-to-back, though רב חמא says gaps are fine where fields are normally left fallow. Finally, the גמרא asks how a חזקה on a house can be proven day and night: neighbors or unbiased renters can testify, and מר זוטרא says the claimant may demand such proof.

steps.title: The prophet's words are good advice, not a law
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the earlier proof from ירמיה. It shows that the prophet often gives practical advice, as in 'build houses and dwell in them.'
steps.simpleTranslation: If you don't say this, then what is the prophet telling us when he says 'Build houses and live in them, plant gardens and eat their fruit'? Clearly he is just giving good advice. Here too, he is just giving good advice.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is knocking down the earlier attempt to learn the three-year rule of חזקה from a פסוק in ירמיה. It says the prophet was only giving practical advice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא points to another statement of ירמיה, 'build houses and dwell in them,' which is obviously not a halachic rule. If that is just advice, then the פסוק used for the proof can also be just advice. So it cannot serve as a source for a legal three-year period.

keyTerms.meaning: For if you do not say so
What is he saying? (here: it makes no sense as a law)

phrases.english: For if you do not say so,
"Build houses and dwell in them,
and plant gardens and eat their fruit"
what is he saying?
phrases.notes: Meaning: as a law, this makes no sense. Nobody is required to build a house.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא עֵצָה טוֹבָה קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן;
phrases.english: Rather, he is teaching us good advice;

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא נָמֵי – עֵצָה טוֹבָה קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן.
phrases.english: here too, he is teaching us good advice.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the earlier proof from ירמיה (from before this section) for the three-year rule.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole attempt to derive the three-year rule of חזקה from the words of ירמיה.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The prophet's words are practical advice, not halachic rulings, so no legal time period can be learned from them.

steps.title: Support: keeping documents in a clay jar is clearly just advice
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings support that ירמיה's words here are advice: he says to put the documents in a clay vessel so they will last.
steps.simpleTranslation: You can see this is true, because it is written: 'Put them in a clay vessel so that they will last many days.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds backing for the claim from the step before. The instruction to store the deeds in a clay jar is plainly practical advice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Telling someone to store documents in a clay jar so they survive is about protecting them. It is not about any legal deadline. This shows the passage as a whole is practical guidance, which strengthens the rejection of the proof.

keyTerms.meaning: Know (that this is so): a word that brings supporting proof

phrases.english: Know this, for it is written:
"And put them in an earthenware vessel,
phrases.notes: ירמיה 32:14. "Them" are the deeds of the field ירמיה bought.

phrases.english: so that they may last many days."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings support for the claim in step 1 that the prophet is giving advice.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that ירמיה's words in this passage are advice, not law.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ירמיה 32:14, the instruction to store the deeds in a clay vessel so they will last.

steps.title: רבא: a person forgives two years but not three
steps.stepSummary: With no פסוק as a source, רבא gives a logical reason for three years: an owner may let someone use his land for one or two years, but not for three.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: The first year, a person lets it go. Two years, he lets it go. Three years, he does not let it go.
steps.whatsHappening: Now that the source from ירמיה is gone, רבא gives a new reason for the three-year rule, based on how people normally behave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא says an owner might forgive (מחיל) another person's use of his field for a year or two. Nobody forgives for three years. So if the owner stays silent through three years, it shows the land is really not his.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather: dropping the earlier approach for a new one

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
The first year, a person waives (his rights);
two (years), he waives;
three, he does not waive.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected proof from a פסוק with a reason based on logic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The three-year rule comes from human behavior: a person waives his rights to his land for up to two years, but not for three.

steps.title: אביי: then the first two years' produce should stay with the user
steps.stepSummary: אביי challenges רבא: if the owner forgave the first two years, then when the land goes back to him, the produce from those years should not have to be returned. Yet רב נחמן ruled that the produce is returned too.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: If so, when the land is returned, it should be returned without the produce! Why then did רב נחמן say: the land is returned and the produce is returned?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי attacks רבא's reason by showing that it clashes with an accepted ruling of רב נחמן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the owner truly forgave the first two years, then the user rightfully ate that produce. If the user then fails to prove ownership and has to give back the land, he should keep what was forgiven. But רב נחמן ruled that the produce is returned along with the land, so the owner never truly forgave anything.

keyTerms.meaning: If so (introduces a challenge from the logic of what was just said)

steps.confusionAlert: אביי is not asking about a case where the user has a full three-year חזקה. He means a case where the user loses and the land goes back to the owner. In that case, the produce from the first two years should be the user's if the owner had truly forgiven it.

phrases.english: Abaye said to him:
If that is so,
when the land is returned,
let it be returned except for the produce!
phrases.notes: He means the produce of the first two years, which the owner supposedly forgave.

phrases.english: Why then did Rav Nachman say:
The land is returned and the produce is returned?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's reason from step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's claim that a person forgives (מחיל) the use of his land for the first two years.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the owner forgave, the produce of those years should belong to the user. But רב נחמן rules that the produce is returned with the land, which shows there was no forgiving.

steps.title: רבא revised: a person doesn't bother protesting until the third year
steps.stepSummary: רבא rewords his reason. The owner does not forgive anything. He just doesn't bother to protest for two years, but in the third year he does.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: The first year, a person is not particular. Two years, he is not particular. Three years, he is particular.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers אביי's challenge by changing 'he forgives' to 'he doesn't bother.' This keeps his reasoning in line with רב נחמן's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Not being particular' (לא קפיד) means the owner doesn't make a fuss yet, but he still has all his rights, including to the produce. So the produce can still be returned, as רב נחמן said. By the third year a real owner would protest, so staying silent then shows the land is not his.

keyTerms.meaning: Doesn't bother / lets it slide (without giving up his rights)

steps.whatToRemember: Three years of חזקה is not learned from ירמיה's words, which were only advice. רבא's second reason, that an owner doesn't bother protesting for two years, fixes the problem about the produce. But it is not the final reason: אביי challenges it in the next step, and רבא replaces it with the deed reason in step 7.
steps.whyThisMatters: The difference between 'forgiving' and 'not bothering' decides whether the produce must be returned. It shows how the reason behind a rule can change its practical results.

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
The first year, a person is not particular (to protest);
two (years), he is not particular;
three, he is particular.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's challenge in step 4 by rewording רבא's reason from step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rewording the reason: from giving up rights to simply not protesting.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The owner forgives the use of his land for two years, so the produce would belong to the user.
steps.terutzMaskana: The owner keeps all his rights and just doesn't bother to protest for two years. So the produce is returned (as רב נחמן said), and silence in the third year shows the land is not his.

steps.title: אביי: Some owners protest right away, so the time would change for each person
steps.stepSummary: אביי challenges רבא's reason that owners protest by the third year. Some owners, like the family of בר אלישיב, protest immediately. Would חזקה then come at once for them? That would make the rule different for every person.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to רבא: If that is your reason, think about the family of בר אלישיב. They get upset even when someone walks along the edge of their field. Would חזקה be made against them right away? And if you say yes, then you have made the rule depend on each person, with a different time for everyone!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי attacks רבא's latest reason, that an owner holds back for two years but protests in the third.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If חזקה depends on when an owner would normally protest, then very strict owners would protest at once. Their silence would create חזקה immediately. That would turn a fixed three-year rule into a different time for each owner, and אביי rejects that as unworkable.

keyTerms.meaning: "If that is so…" (a formula that pushes someone's reasoning to a problem)
Presumed ownership created by using land for three years
The boundary or edge of a field
You have made your rule depend on varying amounts, a different measure for each case

phrases.english: Abaye said to him: If that is so,
such as those of the household of bar Elyashiv,
who are strict even about someone
who just walks along their boundary,
would presumed ownership be made immediately there too?
And if you say, yes, that is so,
then you have made your words depend on measures!
phrases.notes: He means each owner would need a different length of time, and that can't be right.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reworded reason רבא gave in step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's reason that an owner holds back for two years but protests in the third.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the timing depends on the owner's nature, strict owners would make חזקה happen at once, and a fixed shared rule would disappear.

steps.title: רבא's new reason: A buyer guards his deed for three years
steps.stepSummary: רבא drops his earlier reason. Instead he says a buyer is careful to keep his deed of sale for up to three years and no longer. So after three years, his חזקה protects him in place of the deed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Instead, רבא said: In the first year, a person is careful with his deed. In the second and third years he is still careful. After that, he is not careful anymore.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a completely new reason for the three years, this time based on the buyer instead of the original owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new reason looks at how ordinary people treat their documents. People keep a deed safe for about three years, then may lose or throw it away. So we can't demand a deed after that, and three years of use takes its place. This standard is the same for everyone, so אביי's last objection no longer applies.

keyTerms.meaning: A document, here the deed showing that the land was bought

steps.whyThisMatters: This reason treats חזקה as a stand-in for a lost deed. That is why the next challenge is about whether the buyer knew he needed to keep his deed.

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
In the first year a person is careful with his deed,
for two and three years he is careful,
beyond that he is not careful.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the objection in step 6, רבא replaces his reason about the owner's protest with a reason about the buyer guarding his deed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Three years is the length of time a buyer normally keeps his deed safe. After that, his use of the land proves ownership instead.

steps.title: אביי: Then a protest made when the buyer isn't there should not count
steps.stepSummary: אביי challenges the deed reason. If the point is that the buyer stops guarding his deed, he could say: 'You never protested in front of me, so I didn't know to keep my deed.' Then a protest made when he isn't present would not count, but it does count.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: If that is so, a protest made when the buyer is not there should not count as a protest. The buyer could say: 'If you had protested in front of me, I would have kept my deed safe!'
steps.whatsHappening: אביי attacks רבא's new reason by pointing to a problem with protests made when the buyer is not present.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under the deed reason, a protest matters because it warns the buyer to hold on to his deed. A protest made elsewhere would not warn him, so it should not stop his חזקה. אביי treats that result as unacceptable, since such a protest does count.

keyTerms.meaning: A protest, the owner declaring that the land is still his
In front of me, in my presence

phrases.english: Abaye said to him: If that is so,

phrases.aramaic: מֶחָאָה שֶׁלֹּא בְּפָנָיו – לָא תִּיהְוֵי מֶחָאָה,
phrases.english: a protest not made in his presence should not be a protest,
phrases.notes: "His" means the person living on the land. The problem is that such a protest does count.

phrases.english: because he can say to him: Had you protested in front of me,
I would have been careful with my deed!

steps.triggerLanguage: אמר ליה אביי: אלא מעתה, מחאה שלא בפניו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the new deed reason from step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's reason that חזקה replaces a deed people stop guarding after three years.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a protest works only by warning the buyer to keep his deed, a protest he never heard about should not work. Yet it does count.

steps.title: News of a protest spreads, so the buyer is expected to hear
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא defends רבא. The owner can answer: 'Your friend has a friend, and your friend's friend has a friend.' Word of the protest travels and reaches the buyer, so he should have kept his deed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because the owner can say to him: Your friend has a friend, and your friend's friend has a friend.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers אביי's challenge, so רבא's deed reason stands.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A protest made in front of other people does not stay secret. It passes from person to person until it reaches the buyer. So the buyer is treated as having been warned, and he can't claim he didn't know to keep his deed.

keyTerms.meaning: "Your friend has a friend": word gets around and will reach you

steps.whatToRemember: The final reason for three years is the deed: people keep their deeds safe for about three years. A protest counts even when the buyer isn't there, because news spreads and will reach him.
steps.confusionAlert: This line is not אביי speaking. It is the גמרא's answer, telling us what the original owner can say back to the buyer.

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר לֵיהּ: חַבְרָךְ חַבְרָא אִית לֵיהּ,
phrases.english: Because he can say to him: Your friend has a friend,
phrases.notes: The original owner is now answering the buyer's complaint from the last step.

phrases.english: and your friend's friend has a friend.

steps.triggerLanguage: דאמר ליה: חברך חברא אית ליה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's challenge from step 8 and keeps רבא's reason from step 7.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Denies the buyer's claim: a protest made elsewhere is assumed to reach him.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A protest made away from the buyer can't warn him, so it shouldn't count.
steps.terutzMaskana: News spreads from friend to friend. The buyer is treated as warned, so the protest counts.

steps.title: The three years must be back-to-back
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא rules that the three years needed for חזקה must be consecutive.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: The three years the חכמים spoke about only count when the person used the field three years in a row.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic with a ruling from רב הונא. To get חזקה, the three years of using the field must come one right after another.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before this, the סוגיא asked why חזקה takes three years. Now רב הונא adds a rule about how to count them. A gap between the years breaks the count.

keyTerms.meaning: He 'ate' them, meaning he used the field and took its produce

phrases.english: Rav Huna said:
The three years that they (the Sages) said
is when he ate (used) them consecutively.
phrases.notes: 'Ate' means he worked the field and took its crops, not that he literally ate anything.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic about how the three years are counted, after the earlier discussion of why חזקה takes three years.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The three years of חזקה must be consecutive.

steps.title: Why say this? The משנה already says it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what רב הונא adds, since the משנה already says 'three years from day to day.'
steps.simpleTranslation: What is he teaching us? We already learned in the משנה: Their חזקה is three years, from day to day!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב הונא. His rule seems to repeat what the משנה already says, so it seems unnecessary.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'From day to day' sounds like it already means one unbroken stretch of three years. If so, רב הונא's rule adds nothing new. This is a challenge to the need for his statement, not to the rule itself.

keyTerms.meaning: What is he teaching us? (Why do we need this statement?)
From day to day, a full stretch of time

phrases.english: What is he teaching us?
We already learned:
Their presumption of ownership is three years from day to day!
phrases.notes: This quotes the משנה at the start of this פרק.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions why רב הונא's rule in step 10 is needed.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for רב הונא's statement
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה's words 'from day to day' already seem to require three unbroken years, so רב הונא's rule would be extra.

steps.title: The משנה could have meant only full years
steps.stepSummary: The משנה's words might only rule out partial years. רב הונא teaches that the years must also be back-to-back.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have thought that 'from day to day' only comes to rule out partial years, but scattered years would really still count. So רב הונא teaches us that they must be consecutive.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the משנה alone leaves room for a mistake, and רב הונא prevents it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two separate questions: must each year be complete, and must the years come in a row? 'From day to day' clearly answers the first one. רב הונא adds the second rule: the years cannot be spread out with gaps between them.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said (a mistaken idea the statement rules out)
Scattered years with gaps between them

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up 'partial' (מקוטעות) with 'scattered' (מפוזרות). Partial means a year that isn't complete. Scattered means full years with gaps between them. The משנה rules out the first. רב הונא rules out the second.

phrases.english: You might have said
that 'from day to day' comes to exclude partial years
but really even scattered years count;
so he teaches us (that they must be consecutive).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 11 by showing the משנה is not enough without רב הונא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the earlier source is open to a narrower reading, so the new statement adds something
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'From day to day' only requires full years, so scattered full years would count.
steps.terutzMaskana: The three full years must also be consecutive.

steps.title: רב חמא: Fallow-field places are different
steps.stepSummary: רב חמא says רב הונא agrees that in places where fields are left empty every other year, non-consecutive years still count.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חמא said: And רב הונא agrees that in places where people leave fields fallow, the years count even with gaps.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חמא makes an exception to רב הונא's rule. Where it is normal to rest a field every other year, the gaps don't break the חזקה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: חזקה is built on using the field the way an owner normally would. If owners there rest their fields every other year, the holder's skipped years look exactly like an owner's. So the rule about consecutive years still stands, but this case works differently.

keyTerms.meaning: They leave a field fallow, unplanted for a year

phrases.english: Rav Chama said:
And Rav Huna agrees
in places where they leave fields fallow.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חָמָא: וּמוֹדֵי רַב הוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits רב הונא's rule from step 10 with an exception.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Where fields are normally left fallow in alternate years, non-consecutive years of use still make a חזקה.

steps.title: Isn't that obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רב חמא needed to say something so obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: That's obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא objects that רב חמא's point seems too obvious to need saying. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If everyone in a place rests fields every other year, of course the holder did nothing strange. So why state it? The גמרא will answer by narrowing the case.

phrases.english: It's obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges whether רב חמא's statement in step 13 is needed.
steps.kashyaTarget: The need for רב חמא's statement
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Where fallowing is normal, it is plainly the owner's way of using the field, so the ruling seems to teach nothing.

steps.title: A place where only some leave fields fallow
steps.stepSummary: The ruling is needed where some people rest their fields and some don't. The holder can say he couldn't guard one planted plot alone.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed where some people leave fields fallow and some don't, and this man left his fallow. You might have thought the claimant can say: 'If it were really yours, you would have planted it.' So רב חמא teaches that the holder can answer: 'I can't guard one planted plot in the middle of a whole empty field.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that רב חמא is talking about a mixed place. There, leaving a field empty could look suspicious, but the holder has a good answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The claimant argues that a real owner would have planted every year, so the empty years show it wasn't his. The holder answers that the plots around him were empty that year. A single planted plot among them would be hard to protect, so resting it was a sensible owner's choice.

keyTerms.meaning: No, it is needed (for a specific case)
To sow it, to plant it

phrases.english: No, it is needed
where there are those who leave fallow and there are those who do not leave fallow
and this man left it fallow;
you might have said that he can say to him:
phrases.notes: The first 'he' is the person claiming the field. 'Him' is the one holding it.

phrases.english: If it were really yours,
you should have sown it;
so he teaches us that he can say to him:
one plot of land within the whole field
I am not able to guard.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the 'obvious' challenge of step 14 by narrowing רב חמא's case to a mixed place.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrows the case to a situation where the ruling is not obvious
steps.terutzHavaAmina: In a mixed place, leaving the field empty weakens the חזקה, since a real owner would have planted.
steps.terutzMaskana: The holder can explain that guarding one planted plot among empty ones is impractical, so the gap years still count.

steps.title: Another answer: resting the land makes it grow more
steps.stepSummary: A second explanation the holder can give: resting the field every other year makes it produce more.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or else the holder can say: 'This way suits me, because the land produces more.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a second reason the holder can give for leaving the field empty in a mixed place.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer does not depend on the neighbors at all. Resting the soil makes it stronger, so a careful owner might choose to farm every other year. Either way, the empty years fit how an owner acts, and the חזקה holds.

keyTerms.meaning: It suits me, it is better for me

steps.whatToRemember: The three years of חזקה must normally be back-to-back. But if the holder skipped years the way an owner reasonably might, like resting the field, the gaps don't break the count.

phrases.english: And alternatively,
in this way it is good for me
because it produces more.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second reason for the holder, alongside the guarding reason in step 15.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Alternative justification for the same ruling
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A real owner would plant every year.
steps.terutzMaskana: Resting the land is a legitimate farming choice, so the holder's gap years are normal owner behavior.

steps.title: How can anyone testify about a house at night?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב הונא's rule using the משנה's case of houses: witnesses only know who lives in a house by day, not at night.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in the משנה: there is a חזקה for houses. But with houses, people know who uses them during the day. At night they do not know!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a problem with the rule that the years must be back-to-back. It points out that witnesses cannot see inside a house at night.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא said the three years must be continuous with no gaps. A house is normally watched only by day, so every night looks like a gap in the proof. If that is true, how can the משנה say a house can ever get a חזקה?

keyTerms.meaning: Proving ownership of houses by living in them for three years

steps.confusionAlert: The problem is not that people are away at night. The problem is that the witnesses cannot see who is in the house at night, so they cannot testify that the use was nonstop.

phrases.english: We learned: the presumption of ownership of houses.
phrases.notes: This quotes the opening words of our משנה, which lists houses among things that can get a חזקה.

phrases.english: But houses, where by day they know,
at night they do not know!
phrases.notes: 'They' means the witnesses. They cannot tell who is living in the house at night.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies רב הונא's rule of back-to-back years to the משנה's case of houses and finds a problem.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's rule that a חזקה needs continuous, uninterrupted use
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Witnesses only see a house by day. The nights look like gaps, so the use can never be shown as continuous, yet the משנה says houses can have a חזקה.

steps.title: Neighbors know who lives there day and night
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that the witnesses for houses are the neighbors, and neighbors know who is in the house both day and night.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: Who testifies about houses? Neighbors. And neighbors know what goes on by day and by night.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the question. The witnesses for a house are its neighbors, and they know who lives there around the clock.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question assumed the witnesses were outsiders who only see the house by day. אביי says the right witnesses are neighbors, who hear and notice who comes and goes even at night. So the use can be shown as continuous after all.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
Who testifies about houses? Neighbors;
neighbors certainly know, by day and by night.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge about houses at night.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Witnesses only see a house by day, so the nights break the continuity.
steps.terutzMaskana: Neighbors are the witnesses, and they know who is in the house both day and night.

steps.title: Renters can testify they lived there day and night
steps.stepSummary: רבא gives another answer: two renters testify that they rented the house from the holder and lived there for three years, day and night.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: For example, when two people come and say: We rented the house from him, and we lived in it for three years, by day and by night.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a second answer to the question about houses. Witnesses who rented the house from the holder can testify, since they themselves lived in it day and night.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A renter living in the house counts as the holder using it, because the renter is there with his permission. These renters were inside every night, so they can confirm the use was nonstop for three full years.

phrases.english: Rava said:
For example, where two people come and say:
We rented it from him,
phrases.notes: 'From him' means from the holder, the one claiming he owns the house.

phrases.aramaic: וְדָרֵינַן בֵּיהּ תְּלָת שְׁנִין בִּימָמָא וּבְלֵילְיָא.
phrases.english: and we lived in it three years, by day and by night.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אָמַר: כְּגוֹן דְּאָתוּ בֵּי תְרֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, different answer to the same challenge, alongside אביי's.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A specific case where witnesses know about the nights
steps.terutzHavaAmina: No witness can know who is in a house at night.
steps.terutzMaskana: Renters who lived in the house under the holder were there every night and can testify to three continuous years.

steps.title: The renters are biased witnesses
steps.stepSummary: רב יימר objects to רבא: the renters are biased, because if they do not back the holder, they would have to pay rent again to the other claimant.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יימר said to רב אשי: These renters are biased in their testimony. If they do not say this, we would tell them: Go pay rent for the house to this other person!
steps.whatsHappening: רב יימר challenges רבא's answer. He says the renters cannot be trusted, because they gain from their own testimony.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The renters already paid rent to the holder. If the holder is not the real owner, the true owner could make them pay rent again. So they want the holder to win, which makes them נוגעין בעדותן, people with a personal stake whose testimony is not accepted.

keyTerms.meaning: Biased: they have a personal stake in their own testimony

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a basic rule of testimony: a witness who gains from the outcome cannot testify, even if what he says is true.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב יֵימַר לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rav Yeimar said to Rav Ashi:
These are biased in their testimony,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאִי לָא אָמְרִי הָכִי, אָמְרִינַן לְהוּ:
phrases.english: for if they do not say this, we would say to them:

phrases.aramaic: זִילוּ הַבוּ לֵיהּ אֲגַר בֵּיתָא לְהַאי!
phrases.english: Go give the rent of the house to this one!
phrases.notes: 'This one' is the person challenging the holder and saying the house is his. The renters would have to pay him rent too.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבא's answer from the step before.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's case where the renters serve as witnesses
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The renters gain from backing the holder, since otherwise they would owe rent a second time to the real owner, so their testimony is biased and not accepted.

steps.title: The renters are not biased if they still hold the rent money
steps.stepSummary: The responder admits that biased renters would not be accepted by good judges. He explains that רבא's case is renters who have not paid rent yet and are only asking whom to pay, so they have nothing to gain.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Only low-level judges rule like that. But aren't we talking about renters who are still holding the rent money and are asking, 'To whom should we give it?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers רב יימר's objection from Step 20 and saves רבא's case of renters as witnesses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יימר said renters are biased, because siding against the holder would mean paying rent twice. The answer agrees that biased witnesses are not accepted. But if the renters have not paid yet, they pay the same amount whoever wins, so they have no reason to lie.
steps.confusionAlert: The line 'low-level judges rule like that' does not reject רבא. It agrees that biased renters would be wrong to accept, and then shows that רבא meant a case where the renters are not biased at all.

phrases.english: He said to him:
phrases.notes: This is רב אשי answering רב יימר.

phrases.english: Low-level judges rule this way.
Are we not dealing with
a case where they are holding the house rent,
and they are saying: To whom shall we give it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב יימר's objection (Step 20) against רבא's answer (Step 19).
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: the renters have not yet paid rent, so they are not biased.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Renters who already paid the holder would have to pay again if he loses, so they are biased.
steps.terutzMaskana: Renters still holding the rent pay the same no matter who wins, so their testimony is valid.

steps.title: The owner may demand proof of living there day and night
steps.stepSummary: מר זוטרא rules that if the claimant demands that the holder bring two witnesses showing he lived in the house three years, day and night, this is a fair demand.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר זוטרא said: If the claimant argues, 'Let two witnesses come and testify for him that he lived in the house three years, by day and by night,' his claim is a valid claim.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a related ruling of מר זוטרא about what the holder of a house must prove.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier the גמרא worried that witnesses only see who lives in a house by day. מר זוטרא says the claimant may insist on full proof: witnesses that the holder lived there both day and night for three years. Without that, the holder's חזקה is not enough.

keyTerms.meaning: his claim is a valid claim

steps.whatToRemember: For a house, a חזקה needs proof that the holder lived there three full years, day and night. Neighbors or unbiased renters can provide that proof, and the claimant may demand it.
steps.whyThisMatters: It sets a practical rule: the person challenging the holder can insist on full day-and-night testimony, and the court must take that demand seriously.

phrases.english: Mar Zutra said:
And if he claims and says:
phrases.notes: The one claiming is the person challenging the holder, saying the house is really his.

phrases.english: Let two witnesses come to testify for him
that he lived in it three years
by day and by night,
his claim is a valid claim.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר מָר זוּטְרָא, וְאִי טָעֵין וְאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a related practical ruling to the discussion about proving a חזקה on houses day and night.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A claimant may demand that the holder bring two witnesses that he lived in the house three years, day and night, and the court accepts this demand.
